title: The first sign (John 2:1–11)
hook: John calls miracles signs: they point past themselves

segments.voice: Yesterday, under the fig tree: a skeptic asked whether anything good could come from Nazareth. Your line was can any good thing come. Which place or person did you give a second look? Day four hundred ninety-six.

A road sign that says Chicago, 40 miles is not Chicago. Nobody pulls over and takes a selfie with it as if they've arrived. Its whole job is to point somewhere else. Today's word is sign, and it's the word John chooses, again and again, for what the Douay-Rheims calls miracles. He calls them signs. And the first one happens somewhere you wouldn't expect: not in the temple, not at a sickbed, but at a village wedding in Cana of Galilee, on the third day, when the wine runs out.
screen: `A ROAD SIGN ISN'T THE CITY.` → `JOHN'S WORD FOR MIRACLES.` → `A WEDDING IN CANA.`

segments.voice: Mary is the one who speaks up. She says to her son, in the Douay-Rheims: "They have no wine." Just that. His answer sounds cool to our ears: woman, what is that to me and to thee? my hour is not yet come. Woman is the same word he will use for her from the cross, and Mary seems to hear something other than no. She turns to the servants: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." They're her last recorded words in John's Gospel. There are six stone water jars, used for the Jewish rites of washing, each holding two or three measures. Fill them with water, he says. They fill them to the brim. Draw some out, and take it to the steward. The steward tastes it, has no idea where it came from, and calls the bridegroom over: everyone serves the good wine first, and the poorer wine once the guests have drunk well, "But thou hast kept the good wine until now." John closes it this way: "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee; and manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him." Where the Douay says miracles, John's Greek says signs, semeia. It's the word John keeps using. A sign isn't the destination. It points to who he is. Here, water for washing becomes wine for a feast, from jars filled to the brim. Saint John Paul the Second made Cana one of the Luminous Mysteries of the rosary, so those who pray the rosary come back to this wedding, and to Mary's words to the servants.
screen: `THEY HAVE NO WINE.` · `WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY, DO YE.` · `SIX JARS, FILLED TO THE BRIM.` · `NOT A MIRACLE ONLY, A SIGN.` · then, large: `THE GOOD WINE UNTIL NOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for a sign in your day. Settle, and breathe. Go back over today slowly, like flipping through photos on your phone. Look for one small thing that pointed past itself. A kindness that came out of nowhere. A meal that tasted better than it should. A moment that felt like more than it was. Don't force it into anything big. Just notice where it pointed. If you pray, you can thank God for it. If you don't, just let it be a sign of something good. The bell holds the time.
Sign. John's word for Jesus's miracles, semeion in Greek: a deed that points past itself to who he is. The first was at Cana. Today's word.
Your line: the good wine until now. Today, save something good for later in the day, a call, a treat, a kind word, and give it when people least expect it. Day four hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Wedding at Cana as the second of the Luminous Mysteries of the rosary, usually on Thursdays, and often take Mary's words to the servants as a short summary of her role.

fork.setup: you're Mary at a wedding. the wine has run out at the feast. your son has just said his hour is not yet come. what do you do?
options: drop it and say nothing more.
tell the servants: do whatever he tells you.
fork.reveal: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." the water becomes wine, and the steward says the good wine was kept until now.

original.note: Greek: a sign, a mark that points beyond itself. John's word for Jesus's miracles.

trapdoor: what you thought: a party trick that kept the wine flowing.
what it means: the first of John's signs, showing his glory, so his disciples believed in him.
what a scholar hears: semeion, not dynamis (power), is John's word; the Douay's 'miracles' translates the Vulgate's signa.

sources.ref: John Paul II, Rosarium Virginis Mariae 21 (2002)

notes: Jar capacity: two or three 'measures' (metretai), each about 9 US gallons, giving roughly 18–27 gallons per jar. Stated as 'something like twenty or thirty gallons'. Confirm.
Vulgate John 2:11 reads 'initium signorum'; the Douay renders 'beginning of miracles'. Confirm the trapdoor note.
'Her last recorded words in John's Gospel': Mary speaks nowhere else in John. Confirm.
'Woman' as a respectful address: common commentary view. Confirm.
Luminous Mysteries prayed on Thursdays per Rosarium Virginis Mariae 38. Confirm.
